paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend. The brothers bowed down and said, "We are your slaves!" (Genesis 50:18). Joseph had every reason to hold a grudge, and he didn't. He wept, told them, "Do not be afraid," and then asked, "Am I in the place of God?" (Genesis 50:19).

Now hear me, because this is the heart of it. Joseph says, "As for you, what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people." (Genesis 50:20). The brothers meant it for evil, and Joseph never pretends they didn't. But God was working a bigger plan right through the very thing that hurt. So when your life has a chapter you can't make sense of, you can hold it up to God instead of holding it against somebody.

And look at how Joseph finishes. His last words are not about Egypt, where he was second only to Pharaoh. They are about a promise: "God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." (Genesis 50:24). His body sits in a coffin in Egypt, and he's still trusting God to keep His word. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, friend, and I can tell you God doesn't lose track of what He promised, so you can forgive freely and wait with hope. Genesis ends here, but the story of God's promise isn't over.
